title: From a Topic to a Sharp Question
why: A topic is a place to look. A question is a job to do. Researchers spend real time sharpening their question before they start, because a sharp question tells them which facts matter and which they can skip.
A good question also points to how you could find the answer: by reading, by asking people, or by measuring something yourself. Later on this ladder you will do all three.
ai: Not in this unit. You are still practicing questions. From Stage 2 you may ask an AI, then check what it says in two other places.

steps.title: The question funnel
text: Start wide and get narrower in three steps: a topic, one part of the topic, then a question about that part.
Each step leaves things out on purpose. That is what makes the question possible to answer.

examples.label: A sharp question
examples.text: Why does lightning strike tall things, like trees and towers, more often than the ground around them?

examples.label: Smaller questions
examples.text: What is lightning? How does it pick a path to the ground? How does a lightning rod protect a building?

steps.title: Question starters that open research
text: Some ways of starting a question lead to research more often than others. Try these when a question feels flat.

examples.label: How does ... work?
examples.text: How does a lightning rod keep a building safe?

examples.label: Why does ... happen?
examples.text: Why do honeybees sometimes leave their hive and start a new one?

examples.label: What changed when ...?
examples.text: What changed for farmers when tractors replaced horses?

examples.label: How are ... and ... different?
examples.text: How are the lives of frogs and toads different?

examples.label: What happens if ...?
examples.text: What happens to a bean plant's growth if it gets only half as much light?

steps.title: Find the sharpest question
steps.intro: Your first answer is your score.

options: What do you know about the ocean?
How do sea turtles find the beach where they hatched?

questions.hint: Which one names one thing and one puzzle?
questions.why: It names one animal and one puzzle. The other two are so wide that you would not know where to start.

options: What were the Olympics like long ago?
Why did ancient Greek cities agree to stop fighting during the Olympic Games, and did it work?

questions.hint: Which one could you finish answering?
questions.why: It names one custom and asks why and what happened. The others cover too much ground.

options: How does freezing keep food from going bad?
What foods are there in the world?

questions.hint: Which one could you finish answering in a few weeks?
questions.why: It asks how one thing works. The others have no edge.

questions.q: Which question could you answer by measuring something yourself?

options: Is our classroom warmer near the window than near the door during the school day?

questions.hint: Which one could you check yourself with a tool, at school?
questions.why: You could take readings in both places at the same times and compare them.

questions.q: Which question would you answer mostly by asking people?

options: What games do students at my school play most at recess?
How deep is the Pacific Ocean?

questions.hint: Which answer could you not find in a book?
questions.why: Only the students can tell you what they play, so you would ask them.

questions.q: Which question would you answer mostly by reading books and articles?

options: What did people use to keep food cold before refrigerators?
How many steps do I take on a school day?
Which snack do my friends like most?

questions.hint: For which one are the people who know the answer hardest to reach today?
questions.why: It is about the past, so books and articles are the main place to look, though an older relative might remember too. The other two you would measure or ask.

steps.title: The question test
text: Before you keep a question, give it four checks.

examples.label: 1. Can I find out?
examples.text: There are books, people or things to measure that could answer it.

examples.label: 2. Is it more than one fact?
examples.text: The answer takes a few sentences, not one word.

examples.label: 3. Is it the right size?
examples.text: I could answer it in a few weeks, not a lifetime.

examples.label: 4. Do I care?
examples.text: I want to know, so I will keep going when it gets hard.

steps.title: Build your funnel

prev.label: Your best question from last time

text: Use your topic from last time, or a new one if you want. Your best question from last time may already be a sharp question. Put it through the funnel: does it come from one part of your topic? Sharpen it, or start fresh. Build the funnel in your notebook first.

example.label: See an example
lines: Sharp question: How does yeast make bread dough rise, and why does warm dough rise faster than cold dough?
How I could find out: read two articles about yeast, ask a baker, and time two bowls of dough, one warm and one cool.

boxes.label: How I could find the answer
boxes.help: Reading, asking people, measuring, or a mix. Say what you would read, who you would ask, or what you would measure.

steps.title: Test your question
text: Give your sharp question the four checks. For each one, write yes or no and a few words on why.

boxes.label: 2. Is it more than one fact?
My question after the test
boxes.help: If it failed a check, write the fixed question. If it passed all four, write it again.

rows.name: A research question
d: It is a look-up or an opinion question.
Close: it asks how or why, but one fact or one source would almost answer it.
A research question: it needs facts from more than one place.
A clear research question that asks how, why or what changed, and needs facts from several places.

rows.name: The funnel narrows
d: No funnel: the question is as wide as the topic.
The funnel narrows a little, but the question is still too wide.
Each step is narrower, ending in a question he could answer in a few weeks.
Each step leaves something out, and the question names one thing and one puzzle.

rows.name: How to find out
d: A plan that would not answer the question.
A plan that could answer it but is vague about what or whom.
A plan that fits the question and names exactly what to read, who to ask or what to measure.

rows.name: Question test
d: All four checks with short reasons.
All four checks with reasons, and the question fixed where a check failed (or, if all four passed, reasons that show why).

next: Next: Stage 2, sources and notes. You will learn which sources to trust, including how to check what an AI tells you.
